hops.afterHeading: One quality per fibre, or one at a time
hops.title: Miracle berries make sour taste sweet
hops.text: The small red fruit sold as the miracle berry carries a protein called miraculin that tastes flat on its own. Once it has coated the tongue, though, sour drinks can taste sweet, and the effect can last more than an hour. Ayako Koizumi and colleagues worked out why in cultured cells carrying the human sweet receptor. At neutral pH, miraculin weakened the receptor's response to the sweeteners they tested. When they lowered the pH, miraculin switched the receptor on. So with miraculin present, acid recruits the sweet receptor and adds a sweet signal to a drink that should simply be sour.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A halved yellow lemon glistening with golden droplets beside small glossy red berries on a wooden board.
image.caption: Miraculin lets acid switch on the human sweet receptor, so a sour fruit tastes sweet.

hops.afterHeading: Identity and value can be pulled apart
hops.title: Why you still have room for dessert
hops.text: Next time you are too full for one more bite of dinner yet still want dessert, notice that dinner has not lost its flavor. It still tastes familiar; it has lost its appeal. This is sensory-specific satiety, and Edmund Rolls found it while recording a food-responsive neuron in a monkey's hypothalamus. After the monkey had taken a sweet taste to fullness, the neuron went quiet. Rolls pulled a peanut from his pocket, and at the sight of it the neuron fired hard again. In macaques fed to fullness, taste responses in the insula held steady, while neurons farther downstream in orbitofrontal cortex responded less to the food just eaten.

sources.citation: Rolls, Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience 18(1):nsab044 (2023)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A pushed-aside plate of pasta next to a hand reaching toward a bowl of berry sorbet, with a peanut on a napkin.
image.caption: A food can still taste familiar as it loses its appeal, while a different food still sounds good.

hops.title: Salt-hungry mountain goats and hikers' socks
hops.text: In the 1920s a sportsmen's group released twelve mountain goats into Washington's Olympic Mountains, where the species was not native. The herd grew past a thousand animals and ran into a problem: those mountains have no natural salt licks. Hikers became the salt supply. The goats went after sweat, sweaty socks hung to dry and trailside urine, and some followed people for miles. This is salt seeking in the wild, where even a sweaty sock is worth a goat's attention. Between 2018 and 2020, wildlife crews ran four helicopter capture operations and moved 325 goats, in refrigerated trucks, to their native Cascade Range, where mineral licks exist.

sources.citation: National Park Service, Olympic National Park, Summer 2019 Bugler

image.caption: With no salt licks nearby, Olympic mountain goats treated hikers' sweaty gear as a salt source.

audio.title: Salty licorice, warm tongues and plastic bottles
audio.transcript: Three true stories about how a taste begins, how a nerve reports it, and how a single bad experience can make a new taste something an animal avoids. First, a candy from northern Europe. In Scandinavia, people eat salty licorice, which gets its bite from ammonium chloride. Ammonium chloride tastes like a mix of bitter, salty and a little sour. It is generally unpleasant, but people can learn to enjoy it. Taste physiologists have used it for decades as a control stimulus, because it reliably drives a strong response in taste nerves. Yet its mechanism was poorly understood until two thousand twenty-three, when Ziyu Liang, Emily Liman and their colleagues found a major part of the answer in an unexpected place: O T O P one, the same proton channel in type three cells that senses sour acid. Ammonium chloride raises the p H inside the cell, which helps drive protons in through O T O P one and may also help open the channel. Changing one conserved spot on the channel weakened that response. When the team deleted O T O P one in mice, the response of a taste nerve serving the front of the tongue dropped sharply. In a brief licking test, O T O P one and S K N one A double-knockout mice showed no avoidance of the ammonium chloride concentrations tested. Ammonium chloride also activated human O T O P one in cultured cells, suggesting this same acid-sensing channel may help people taste the salt that gives the candy its bite. Second, you might assume a taste fibre speaks up only when a molecule lands on your tongue. Physiologists had long known that as many as half of the neurons in mammalian taste pathways also respond to temperature. In two thousand, Alberto Cruz and Barry Green at Yale tested what that means for people, using no food at all. They touched a clean temperature probe to small spots on volunteers' tongues. Warming the front edge of the tongue from cold could make people taste sweetness out of nothing. Cooling the same edge could evoke sourness or saltiness instead. The back of the tongue answered temperature too, with its own pattern. In some volunteers, a change in temperature alone was enough to evoke a taste. Finally, the early nineteen fifties, and the psychologist John Garcia, who was studying the effects of radiation on laboratory rats. He and his colleagues noticed an odd thing. Rats that had been given water in plastic bottles during radiation exposure afterwards refused to drink from plastic bottles, yet the same rats drank happily from glass ones. Garcia and his colleagues suspected that the plastic gave the water a faint taste the rats had learned to associate with the effects of radiation. To test the idea directly, the team gave rats sweet saccharin water during radiation. After a single pairing, the rats strongly avoided a sweet drink they would normally prefer. The drink was the same. One pairing with radiation was enough to make the rats choose less of it in a later test, showing how quickly they learned to avoid that taste. Put the three together and you have the lesson in miniature. A channel can start a taste signal, nerve fibres carry it onward, and need or experience can change how much a taste appeals.
